profiles.meeting_scenario: The ASP team at an open-source solver project is holding a 45-minute brainstorming meeting about a prototype extension that adds exact rational-number support to their ASP-Core-2 implementation. The immediate context is that they want to turn a recent research idea into a developer-facing prototype for the next experimental release, with motivating examples drawn from game motion, robotic arm kinematics, and streamed sensor values. The agenda is to generate and narrow candidate approaches for how 'native' rational numbers should appear in the language, what a believable demo slice should include, and where in the toolchain normalization and exact arithmetic should live. The expected outcome is a short list of prototype directions plus a rough division of follow-up investigation areas for the design memo.

members.name: Elena Rossi
members.expertise: ASP semantics, grounding pipelines, symbolic rewriting, exact arithmetic representations
members.background: Elena has spent the last six years maintaining the core grounding and solving internals of the team's ASP engine and has co-authored papers on conservative language extensions.
members.private_state: She wants the prototype to stay academically defensible and small enough to implement without destabilizing the solver, and she is worried that broad integration requests will turn a semantics prototype into a product commitment.
hidden_assumptions: A feature counts as native once rational numbers are part of the core language semantics and internal term system, even if peripheral APIs and output tools lag behind.
Unless someone explicitly says otherwise, example use cases like sensors or robotics are modeled as offline fact batches rather than live incremental feeds.
Equivalent rational values should be reduced to a canonical form as early as possible, ideally during parsing or grounding, because indexing and equality in the solver assume normalized terms.
Reproducibility primarily means that stable models and entailments are mathematically identical across machines, not that every printed artifact is byte-for-byte the same.
Compatibility with ASP-Core-2 means existing integer-only programs preserve their meaning unchanged under a conservative extension.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.expertise: Developer tooling, Python APIs, incremental solving workflows, benchmark automation
members.background: Marcus supports internal teams who embed the solver in simulation and monitoring systems, and he regularly turns research features into usable command-line and API capabilities.
members.private_state: He wants the prototype to feel usable to application teams immediately and is concerned that a narrow semantics-first demo will be dismissed as impractical if it cannot plug into the existing streaming harness and regression tooling.
hidden_assumptions: Users only experience a feature as native if they can pass it through the CLI, Python API, model printer, and incremental session interfaces without custom wrappers.
Reproducibility for the team means CI logs, saved models, and demo outputs are identical strings across machines and reruns because downstream automation compares artifacts directly.
When people cite streamed sensors as a target domain, that naturally includes the existing incremental ingestion harness rather than only static batches of facts.
Canonicalization should happen late enough that the system can preserve the user's original numeric spelling in logs and debugging output.
Interface conventions for experimental numeric syntax are mostly inherited from the team's earlier decimal-literal discussions and do not need to be reopened unless there is a problem.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both participants discuss adding 'native rational support' to the solver.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means rationals become first-class objects in the formal language and solver internals, without relying on external floating-point preprocessing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means users can enter, inspect, and manipulate rationals end-to-end through the parser, CLI output, Python bindings, and incremental interfaces.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In solver discussions, 'native' sounds like an obviously shared aspiration, and both oppose floating-point hacks, so the phrase creates a strong false sense of agreement without forcing anyone to spell out which layers are included.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both participants say the prototype must be 'reproducible.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means two compliant runs on different machines produce the same mathematical stable models and truth conditions, even if representation details are not the focus.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means repeated runs must emit identical printed rationals, logs, and regression artifacts so automation and demos compare cleanly.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Reproducibility is a universally positive research term, and both treat it as non-negotiable, so neither thinks to probe whether they are aligning on semantic equivalence or artifact-level identity.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both participants talk about using a 'sensor-stream example' to motivate the prototype.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 imagines a static benchmark made from timestamped sensor readings loaded as ordinary facts, just rich enough to show exact rational arithmetic in rules.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 imagines the prototype being exercised through the existing incremental stream harness that ingests new readings continuously.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'sensor-stream example' sounds concrete enough that each person assumes the practical setup is obvious from team context, even though one is imagining an offline encoding and the other a live integration path.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both participants agree that the system should 'canonicalize fractions.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes eager normalization during parsing or grounding so values like 2/4 and 1/2 collapse early for joins, indexing, and semantic cleanliness.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes late normalization only when comparing or serializing values so user-written forms remain visible in ASTs, traces, and debugging views.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Canonicalization sounds like a low-level implementation hygiene step rather than a design fork, so both feel comfortable using the same word while silently importing different execution plans.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this scoped as a semantics prototype, not let it balloon into a platform-wide commitment. For me, native rational support means rationals are first-class in the language and internal term machinery, with exact arithmetic all the way through grounding and solving. If we can show that as a conservative extension to ASP-Core-2, that's already a solid experimental release, even if some peripheral interfaces catch up later.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. What I'd like from this session is a realistic first cut at native rational support for the experimental release—something we can defend cleanly from the language and solver side without compromising the declarative story. We should brainstorm broadly for a bit, then narrow to a prototype slice that is small enough to build and still says something meaningful.

turns.inner_thought: If this lands as just a semantics demo with hand-fed files, application teams will shrug. We need a sensor-stream example that runs through the same incremental ingestion setup people already use, otherwise 'native' won't feel real. I don't need to say all that yet; Elena will probably assume we're aligned once I anchor on the use case.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, I think the release will land much better if it's anchored in a sensor-stream example and not only in toy arithmetic encodings. If people can see a familiar workflow behind the idea, it'll be easier to justify why native rational support matters.

turns.inner_thought: Good, a sensor-stream example is fine as motivation as long as we don't let the infrastructure dictate the core design. The key is a conservative extension: rational literals, exact operators, unchanged meaning for all existing integer-only programs. And reproducible behavior means the same stable models and entailments regardless of machine details.
turns.utterance: Agreed. The cleanest path I see is a conservative language extension: rational literals, exact arithmetic operators, and no surprises for existing integer-only programs. If we do that, the non-negotiable constraint is reproducible behavior across machines. I don't want anything about this prototype to depend on implementation accidents.

turns.inner_thought: Reproducible absolutely has to include emitted artifacts. If logs, printed models, or saved outputs vary, CI and downstream demos become a mess, even if the underlying answers are mathematically the same. I should tie that to practical workflow, but keep it framed as obvious support for her point.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely on reproducible behavior. It also makes the demo and the regression side much easier if model printouts and logs stay stable when users work with rationals. That way the experimental release is easier to exercise and compare in practice.

turns.inner_thought: I should gently keep us away from a full live-system commitment. For a sensor-stream example, a static set of timestamped facts is enough to show exact arithmetic in rules and constraints. That's still faithful to the domain while keeping the prototype academically clean and implementation risk low.
turns.utterance: On the motivating cases, I think the sensor-stream example can stay fairly lean. We could encode timestamped readings as facts and still capture the flavor we need, which lets us focus on the semantics rather than spending most of the effort on surrounding machinery.

turns.inner_thought: Great, she said sensor-stream example and didn't object to the usual path, so I can build on that. Reusing the existing stream harness would let us exercise the feature in the same incremental session flow teams already expect from native rational support, without inventing a special wrapper. That seems like the obvious interpretation of what she just proposed.
turns.utterance: I like keeping it lean. If we can reuse the existing stream harness around that sensor-stream example, we'd get something that exercises the same native rational support path people already recognize, and we'd learn early where the rough edges are.

turns.inner_thought: The key technical choice is normalization. Equivalent rationals must collapse early—ideally at parse or grounding—because solver indexing and equality assumptions get ugly fast otherwise. I'll phrase it as canonicalizing fractions so it sounds like an implementation hygiene decision, not a broad debate.
turns.utterance: One design point I do want on the table early is that we should canonicalize fractions. My instinct is to make equivalent values collapse before they spread through too much of the pipeline, because that usually keeps the core reasoning machinery simpler.

turns.inner_thought: Canonicalizing fractions is fine, but I definitely don't want to lose the original spelling too early. For debugging, AST inspection, and printed traces, users need to recognize what they typed; otherwise support tickets become painful. I can endorse canonicalization while nudging toward preserving visible forms in outputs, and she'll probably take that as just polish.
turns.utterance: Yes, canonicalizing fractions sounds right to me too. I would just want us to do it in a way where users can still recognize the forms they typed when they're looking at traces or outputs, especially if we're aiming for reproducible behavior in demos and checks.

turns.inner_thought: Time to narrow this down before it drifts. The prototype should be parser plus grounder plus exact arithmetic semantics, with a compact benchmark set: maybe motion, kinematics, and a sensor-stream example encoded simply. I am intentionally not promising full API, printer, or incremental coverage; those can be investigated separately if needed.
turns.utterance: Let me try to compress what seems workable. A promising prototype direction is parser-plus-grounder support with exact arithmetic semantics, paired with a compact motivating benchmark suite—say one motion example, one kinematics example, and one sensor-stream example. That feels like enough to make native rational support concrete without turning the first release into a giant integration project.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I can run with that and fill in the rest from the user-facing side. I'll assume the prototype should cover the standard CLI, Python, output, and incremental workflow because otherwise the examples and regressions won't reflect how teams actually use it. I don't need to spell that out; 'user-facing examples and checks' should be enough.
turns.utterance: That sounds like a good shortlist. I can take the first pass on user-facing examples and regression checks, so we have something concrete in the memo about how people would interact with native rational support and how we'll keep it reproducible. Then you can drive the core design notes, and we can compare where the prototype boundaries should sit.
